title: Company-Specific Frameworks
summary: The same underlying competencies get relabeled and weighted differently by every company. Learn how Amazon's Leadership Principles, Google's 'Googleyness,' and Meta's core values differ, and how to map one story bank onto whichever one you're facing.

slides.markdown:
Underneath different branding, most companies score the same handful of underlying competencies: ownership, collaboration, judgment under ambiguity, and (at senior levels) influence and leadership. What changes company to company is the **label**, the **weighting**, and how explicitly the framework is published.

Amazon names 16 Leadership Principles and interviews against them almost word for word. Google talks about "Googleyness" more loosely. Meta scores against a short list of core values. None of this requires a separate story bank per company — it requires remapping the same tagged stories onto whichever vocabulary you're facing.

slides.subTitle: How they're interviewed against
slides.markdown:
Amazon publishes all 16 Leadership Principles (LPs) publicly — Customer Obsession, Ownership, Invent and Simplify, Are Right, A Lot, Bias for Action, Frugality, Earn Trust, Dive Deep, Disagree and Commit, and others. Each interviewer in a loop is typically assigned 2-3 specific LPs to probe, and questions are often written to map directly onto one: "Are Right, A Lot" tends to surface as "tell me about a decision you made with limited data," "Dive Deep" as "a time you found a root cause others missed."

The practical implication: for an Amazon loop specifically, tag your story bank against the LP list directly rather than a generic competency list, and be ready for the interviewer to literally reference the principle name mid-interview ("that sounds like Ownership — tell me more about the outcome").

slides.sectionTitle: Amazon LPs vs. Google's Googleyness vs. Meta's core values
slides.markdown:
| Company | Framework | Character |
|---|---|---|
| Amazon | 16 named Leadership Principles | Explicit, published, interviewed almost literally |
| Google | "Googleyness & Leadership" plus general cognitive ability | Looser, less codified; blends culture-fit signals with problem-solving |
| Meta | A short list of core values (e.g. Move Fast, Be Bold, Focus on Impact) | Explicit but less granular than Amazon's; often folded into a single behavioral round |

The practical takeaway: Amazon rewards explicitly naming the principle in your answer ("this is a Customer Obsession story"); doing the same at Google or Meta can sound stilted, since their frameworks are less about literal recitation. Calibrate the *degree* of explicit framework-naming to the company, not just the content of the story.

slides.sectionTitle: Mapping a single story onto multiple frameworks
slides.markdown:
Take one story from your bank: you shipped a workaround under a tight deadline instead of the ideal fix, and flagged the tech debt for later. Mapped across frameworks:

- **Amazon:** frame as "Bias for Action" (shipped a reversible decision fast rather than waiting for the perfect one) with a secondary nod to "Ownership" (you tracked and later resolved the debt).
- **Google:** frame more generally as pragmatic problem-solving and follow-through — less need to name a specific value, more emphasis on the reasoning behind the trade-off.
- **Meta:** frame as "Move Fast" with the debt follow-through showing you didn't move fast recklessly.

Same facts, same STAR shape — only the framing sentence at the top of the answer changes to speak the company's vocabulary.

slides.sectionTitle: Where to find a target company's stated values
slides.markdown:
Before a loop, spend 15-20 minutes finding the company's actual stated framework rather than guessing:

- The company's careers or "life at" page, which frequently lists values or principles directly.
- The company's own engineering or leadership blog — several companies publish posts explaining how their values show up in day-to-day decisions.
- Glassdoor and Blind interview reviews, filtered to recent behavioral-round accounts, for how the framework actually shows up in practice rather than just its marketing language.
- Your recruiter — asking "what competencies will this round focus on" is a normal, expected question, not a red flag.

Skip generic "top 10 behavioral questions" lists that aren't company-specific; they teach the archetype, covered in the previous topic, not the company's particular framing of it.

slides.sectionTitle: How much company-specific research is actually worth doing
slides.markdown:
There's a real ceiling on the return from this research, and it's worth naming so you don't over-invest. Once you know the company's framework and have remapped your existing tagged stories onto it — typically a 1-2 hour exercise — additional research produces sharply diminishing returns.

What's *not* worth doing: memorizing all 16 Amazon LPs verbatim if you can't also produce a story for each, or building an entirely separate story bank per company. The story bank stays constant; only the framing vocabulary and which 2-3 stories you lead with should shift per company.

Spend the marginal hour instead rehearsing your existing stories' facts and follow-up answers — that consistently matters more than deeper framework trivia.

slides.sectionTitle: Name-dropping a principle with no story behind it
slides.markdown:
A common overcorrection: opening with "this is a great example of Customer Obsession" and then telling a story that doesn't actually demonstrate it — vague on customer impact, no real trade-off made on the customer's behalf. Interviewers who wrote the framework can tell the difference between a story that earns the label and one that's just wearing it.

The fix is sequencing: build the story on its merits first — concrete situation, action, measurable result — then, only if it genuinely fits, name the principle as a one-line frame at the start or end. Never work backward from "I need an Ownership story" to inventing details that force-fit a real incident into the label.

Given a target company, do this once before the loop: take your 8-12 tagged stories, and next to each, write the one or two framework labels (LP name, value name, or general competency) it maps to for that specific company. Circle the 3-4 stories with the strongest, most-defensible mapping — those are your primary answers if given a choice of what to discuss.

This is a 20-30 minute exercise per company, reusing the same underlying bank every time. It's far cheaper than building new material, and it's what actually shows up as fluency in the room: a candidate who speaks the company's specific vocabulary naturally, without sounding like they memorized a glossary the night before.

slides.sectionTitle: Framework fluency isn't the finish line
slides.markdown: Knowing a company's vocabulary makes your answers land better, but it doesn't substitute for scope. The next topic covers a related but distinct axis: how the same story, mapped to the same framework, needs to demonstrate different scope and ownership depending on whether you're interviewing for an entry-level or staff-level role — a dimension that cuts across every company's framework equally.
